performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: The fourth movement of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Scheherazade, Op. 35, moves from a crowded festival to a storm at sea, and the suite’s earlier melodies return together. After the shipwreck, Scheherazade’s violin holds a high note above a quiet E-major chord.

sections.label: Frame · Orchestra alternating with solo violin
sections.mNote: Forceful orchestral calls alternate with the violin’s recitative

sections.label: A · Flute begins the festival dance
sections.mNote: Quick flute notes over a repeated string pulse

sections.label: B · Third-movement dance theme returns
sections.mNote: The third movement’s lighter tune returns within the festival music.

sections.label: A′ · Festival dance theme returns
sections.mNote: Winds and brass join the rushing strings.

sections.label: Dev · Brass fanfares in the dance
sections.mNote: The Kalendar’s brass calls enter the quick music.

sections.label: Sea · Return of the sea theme
sections.mNote: The first movement’s sea music returns in the full orchestra.

sections.label: Close · Brass chords over strings
sections.mNote: Brass chords fade out above the strings.

sections.label: Frame′ · Old melodies in quiet voices
sections.mNote: Woodwind phrases lead to the violin’s final recitative.

sections.label: Coda · High violin over E major
sections.mNote: The violin holds a high note above the final quiet chords.

cues.title: Opening Allegro molto and recitatives
cues.text: Oboes, clarinets, bassoons and strings play the Sultan’s phrase. It stops on a rest, and the solo violin follows with a recitative. Brass and percussion join the next orchestral interruption, and the solo violin plays a second recitative after it.
cues.evidence: Full score, finale, printed pp. 76–79: opening Allegro molto, two Lento recitatives, and the intervening Allegro molto e frenetico. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bass drum in the introduction
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov adds percussion in stages across the suite: timpani first, then cymbals and triangle, then snare drum and tambourine. The bass drum first plays in the introduction to this movement, with the Sultan’s theme. The tam-tam is held back for the shipwreck.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the staged introduction of percussion across the suite and the bass drum in the finale’s introduction, with the tam-tam at the shipwreck. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Festival dance, flute melody
cues.text: At Vivo, the strings begin a quick repeated accompaniment, and a flute plays the festival dance tune above it. At rehearsal A the clarinet and bassoon enter, followed by the triangle.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 79: Vivo, string accompaniment, flute melody, then bassoon, clarinet and triangle at rehearsal A. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the third-movement dance
cues.text: The lighter dance from the third movement, the prince-and-princess movement, returns in the festival as a contrasting theme. Paul Serotsky identified it as the Allegretto from that movement, rescored. Its short phrases are fitted into the faster music.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky identifies the festival’s contrasting theme as the rescored Allegretto from the third movement. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kalender and Princess themes in the festival
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov pointed out that the Kalender’s principal tune and the Princess’s clarinet theme return as secondary themes of the Baghdad festival. He also noted that “nothing is said in The Arabian Nights about these persons taking part in the festivities.”
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition, pp. 247–248, on the recurrence of the Kalender and Princess themes in the Bagdad festival. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Inspector of Navy Bands, 1873
cues.text: In 1873 the composer was appointed Inspector of Music Bands of the Navy. That summer he obtained a trombone, a clarinet and a flute and worked out their fingerings at his summerhouse in Pargolovo, playing them “for all the neighbours to hear”. The post was abolished in 1884.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, translated by Judah A. Joffe, second edition: the appointment and the instruments at Pargolovo, pp. 115–117; release from the post in spring 1884, pp. 226–227. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Kalendar fanfares in the finale
cues.text: The brass fanfares of the Kalendar movement return in the festival music, where they once broke into a bassoon’s tale. The short calls now sound against the quick dance, and the strings continue the dance rhythm beneath them. Paul Serotsky identifies this central episode of the finale as a development of those fanfares.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky identifies the finale’s central episode as a development of the Kalendar movement’s brass fanfares. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the sea music
cues.text: The sea music from the first movement returns, broad and heavy, over rolling figures in the strings. The marking changes to Allegro non troppo maestoso. Woodwind runs and harp glissandi sound against the string figures, and brass and percussion build to the shipwreck.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 132–139: Allegro non troppo maestoso, return of the sea material, harp glissandi, and the tam-tam at the culmination. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The shipwreck, tam-tam
cues.text: The music cuts abruptly to Sinbad’s ship in the storm. The ship’s theme returns in broken fragments in the basses, and the wreck comes on a stroke of the tam-tam. A calm passage follows.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky describes the cut to Sinbad’s ship, the stuttering bass theme, the tam-tam and the stunned calm after the wreck. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The thousand-and-first night
cues.text: Scheherazade leaves each story unfinished so that the Sultan has to wait for the ending. By the thousand-and-first night he has fallen in love with her and abandons his plan to kill her. On the suite’s last pages, the Sultan’s theme returns softened.
cues.evidence: Herbert Glass summarises the story; Serotsky describes the softened Sultan theme at the close. https://www.laphil.com/works/scheherazade ; https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/rimsky_scheheraz.htm

cues.title: Epilogue, clarinet and solo violin
cues.text: At Poco più tranquillo a solo clarinet plays a wave figure over soft strings. Then, at Lento recitativo, the violin and harp return to Scheherazade’s recitative, and the violin ends with a rising cadenza above the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 140–141: Poco più tranquillo, clarinet over strings, followed by Lento recitativo for violin and harp and the rising cadenza. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bob Varney’s transfer, 2009
cues.text: Bob Varney transferred Victor’s original 78-rpm album to digital, and the recording was added to the Internet Archive in 2009. The Wikimedia Commons file description reads: “Transferred and restored from the original 78 set.”
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item Sheherazade: transfer from the original Victor 78 set DM-920 by Bob Varney, added 2009. https://archive.org/metadata/Sheherazade/metadata ; Wikimedia Commons file description: “Transferred and restored from the original 78 set.”

cues.title: Violin high E, closing E major
cues.text: The violin plays a high E above the orchestra. Woodwinds, horns and harp hold the harmony beneath it. The last string chords are pizzicato, in E major, after the heavy opening of the Sultan’s theme.
cues.evidence: Full score, printed p. 142: high violin E, sustained wind and horn harmony, harp chords and final pizzicato strings. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Second violin recitative into the Vivo
transitions.from: Frame · Orchestra alternating with solo violin
transitions.to: A · Flute begins the festival dance
transitions.how: The solo violin’s second recitative slows over held notes in the cellos and basses. At Vivo, horns, percussion and strings set a quick pulse. The flute enters above with the festival tune, and the violas play repeated notes beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 79: second Lento recitative and opening Vivo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf

transitions.title: From the dance to the sea music
transitions.from: Dev · Brass fanfares in the dance
transitions.to: Sea · Return of the sea theme
transitions.how: The short dance figures stop, and the tempo changes to Allegro non troppo maestoso. Violins and cellos play the sea tune from the first movement, and the other strings repeat their accompaniment beneath it. The winds and brass hold broad chords, and the percussion reinforces the returning wave figures.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed p. 132, Allegro non troppo maestoso and the following sea-music return. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf

transitions.title: Brass dies away after the shipwreck
transitions.from: Sea · Return of the sea theme
transitions.how: A tam-tam stroke marks the climax of the shipwreck. Low strings and timpani keep playing beneath the brass, whose held chords are marked morendo (dying away). At Poco più tranquillo the clarinet takes up the wave figure over soft strings and a sustained bass.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 139–140: tam-tam, low-string motion, morendo brass and Poco più tranquillo. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf

transitions.title: The violin holds E above E major
transitions.from: Frame′ · Old melodies in quiet voices
transitions.to: Coda · High violin over E major
transitions.how: The violin’s cadenza climbs into the high register. At Alla breve, Tempo come I, the violin holds a high E while the strings play beneath it. Woodwinds and horns join the closing E-major harmony, and the strings play pizzicato chords while the violin keeps holding its E above them.
transitions.evidence: Full score, printed pp. 141–142, end of the cadenza and Alla breve, Tempo come I. https://archive.org/download/Cantorion_sheet_music_collection_5/ab0957b6477cf0ab933a63817b908c55.pdf

source.title: Rimsky-Korsakov, Scheherazade, IV, full-score scan
source.locator: Printed pp. 76–79: orchestral calls, violin recitatives and opening Vivo; pp. 132–139: sea music and shipwreck; pp. 140–142: clarinet, violin and final E-major chords.

timeline.note: Oboes, clarinets, bassoons and strings play the opening phrase. Flutes, brass and percussion are silent.
The solo violin answers above held cellos and basses; a harp chord joins its recitative.
The second orchestral call brings in piccolo, brass, timpani, triangle and tambourine.
The solo violin plays its second recitative over held notes in the cellos and basses; the harp rests.
Horns, percussion and strings begin the Vivo pulse. The flute starts the dance, then the clarinet and bassoon join.
Piccolo, brass and percussion join the winds and rushing strings.
Woodwinds and strings exchange the lighter dance tune from the third movement.
The festival tune returns, with brass and percussion joining the strings.
The woodwind play phrases above a lighter string accompaniment.
Brass and percussion reinforce the winds and running strings.
The Kalendar’s short fanfares enter the festival dance.
Woodwind and brass join the strings as the festival dance grows louder.
The sea tune returns in violins and cellos, with winds, brass, percussion and harp playing around it.
After the shipwreck, brass chords fade over timpani and low strings.
In the epilogue Scheherazade’s violin recitative returns over harp chords.
Quiet woodwind and string phrases lead to the solo violin’s last cadenza.
The high violin holds above quiet E-major chords in winds, horns, harp and strings.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and professor, known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
